newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan oil, gas deregulation seen still on track.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan oil, gas deregulation seen still on track.

text.p: Pakistan's new government is likely to pursue the oil and gas deregulation policies launched by its predecessor, departing Petroleum and Natural Resources Minister Javed Jabbar said on Tuesday.
"The indications are that the new government shares the broad concerns we have," Jabbar told Reuters in an interview. "They are unlikely to reverse any of our measures."
Jabbar, a member of the caretaker cabinet installed after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5, initiated far-reaching energy sector reforms.

Most were enacted by presidential ordinance and will need eventual endorsement by the newly-elected National Assembly (lower house), which chose industrialist Nawaz Sharif as prime minister on Monday by a staggering vote of 177-16.
Jabbar said his measures to deregulate Pakistan's oil product distribution would increase competition, encourage efficiency and reduce opportunities for corruption.
"The government was playing a role it was not suited for. It should be a regulator, not an operator," he declared.
After a 16-month transition period, the government would end its 30-year-old practice of importing oil products, handing over responsibility to the private sector, Jabbar said.

Last month the caretaker government awarded an oil marketing licence to Attock Petroleum Ltd, enabling it to join the three companies operating for the past 25 years -- state-owned Pakistan State Oil (PSO), which has a 70 percent market share, Shell, with about 23 percent, and Caltex, with six percent.
Jabbar said the government would at the same time strengthen its regulatory role by forming a Petroleum Regulatory Board by the second or third quarter of this year.
A holding company had been set up to separate the Petroleum and Natural Resources Ministry's regulatory functions from its functions as a shareholder in oil and gas exploration ventures.
Other reforms included scrapping a state-subsidised -- and widely abused -- freight mechanism designed to ensure that oil products were sold at uniform prices all over Pakistan.
"It is estimated that we were losing 2.5 billion rupees ($62 million) a year under the freight pool system," Jabbar said. "Its cost was also rising about 30 percent a year."

Freight charges will be frozen during the 16-month transition after which oil marketing firms will arrange their own transport and charge what Jabbar called a "rational and reasonable" price differential in various parts of the country.
Jabbar said the original terms offered to foreign oil and gas exploration companies in 1994 had been restored.
The Bhutto government originally promised that it would charge no more than three percent duty on imported machinery and equipment, but then added customs and regulatory duty in 1995.
"This shattered the confidence of the oil and gas companies...and stalled their activities," Jabbar said.
Jabbar said the caretaker government had also removed a 40 percent cap on profits of the Pak Refinery Company, in which Shell and PSO are major shareholders.
"This has enabled it to go for a $60 million expansion and upgrade of the refinery for the first time in over 30 years," he said. "It can reinvest its profits in the expansion."

Jabbar said the government had restructured the management of state-owned Oil and Gas Development Corporation (OGDC) to give it more decision-making powers and shield it from political interference as a prelude to the sale of a 49 percent stake.
"We are preparing OGDC for partial privatisation," he said. "I estimate that it should be worth in real terms well over $1 billion. Its worth in my opinion should really be $3 billion."
The sale would inject new capital, bring in new management and technology from overseas, and help Pakistan increase investment in oil exploration onshore and offshore.
The caretakers had drafted a new offshore drilling package to attract foreign investment, he said, but gave no details.
